newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Kohl ally - big France deficit could hurt EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kohl ally - big France deficit could hurt EMU.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's top deputy said on Wednesday the launch of a single European currency could run into trouble if France fails to keep its budget deficit under control.

Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and a staunch proponent of the euro, said he hoped the new French government would be successful in working to meet strict deficit targets for the single currency.

But when asked if France's deficit were to reach a level of about 3.6 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), far above the 3.0 percent target Germany is aiming for, Schaeuble said that would be problematic for economic and monetary union (EMU).

"It would be a problem if it came to a budget deficit of this size in France," Schaeuble said in an interview with ZDF television. He added that he hoped France would make serious efforts to limit its budget deficit this year.

Speaking a week after France said it would not meet the 3.0 percent deficit target this year, Schaeuble said that all EMU participants must achieve the EMU targets in 1997 and said Germany also had its work cut out for it to meet the goal.

Many analysts believe Germany's deficit will be slightly above the 3.0 percent threshold, but believe the euro would be launched nevertheless. They say EMU's start could be aborted if deficits in Germany or France are far above 3.0 percent.
In another warning apparently aimed at France, Finance Minister Theo Waigel said all countries joining EMU needed to have the same level of German-style stability.

Waigel wrote in the Bayernkurier, the weekly newspaper of his Christian Social Union (CSU) party, there would be no moral judgment against countries not taking part in EMU, but said the criteria must be reached.

"A chain is only as strong as its weakest link," Waigel wrote. "So, at the beginning of the monetary union, only countries that are equally stable can join. Convergence determines the schedule, in every single country."
He said Maastricht Treaty rules for determining economic convergence among European Union members were indispensible.

Kohl, under pressure to take a hard line on EMU from Bavarian premier and leading Euro-sceptic Edmund Stoiber, made clear on Tuesday that Germany wanted a strict interpretation of the fiscal targets for monetary union.
Kohl tried to silence what German media and politicians have dubbed as the "decimal point debate" by pledging Bonn would meet the 3.0 percent deficit-to-GDP goal on time.

Although normally avoiding precise statements about the Maastricht target, Kohl opted for a clearer stand in a tactical move to blunt Stoiber's campaign and signal to France it could not massively overshoot the deficit criterion.
"We're staying with 3.0 -- that's no problem -- and with the schedule," Kohl said in Munich on Tuesday.

In a speech on Wednesday, Stoiber said he would continue fighting for a strong euro so Germans would have faith in the new currency. He said people would only trust the euro if it were as strong as the mark.

"People want to have something from their savings and we cannot allow inflation to suck that away," said Stoiber, whose play to popular fears about the euro annoyed Kohl and other leaders in Bonn's ruling centre-right coalition.

Gerhard Schroeder, a leading Social Democrat candidate to challenge Kohl in 1998 elections and premier of Lower Saxony state, said in a newspaper interview published in Switzerland on Wednesday the euro may have to be delayed.

"If it is possible to introduce the euro in 1999 with a stability-orientated policy, then good. If it cannot be done without grinding economic, social and political damage, then you have to chose a more favourable time," he told Switzerland's Finanz und Wirtschaft business newspaper.
